Now is the winter of our discontent. This is Richard III's opening soliloquy, in which the deformed, ambitious duke announces his intention to manipulate, seduce, and murder his way to the throne. He frames his ambition as a response to nature's cruelty in making him ugly, casting himself as both victim and villain.

Richard delivers the speech alone on stage at the play's outset, establishing his character and intentions with no intermediary. He opens with the famous line: now is the winter of our discontent. He uses this metaphor to suggest that the Wars of the Roses are ending and peace is dawning, but he will prevent that peace from taking root.

Richard's physical deformity is his defining characteristic. He blames it for his ambition and cruelty, inverting the roles of victim and perpetrator. He announces his seduction plot against Anne, widow of the man he murdered, and his schemes against his brother George and the king. What distinguishes the speech is how Richard establishes himself as charming, witty, self-aware, and utterly amoral. He knows he is evil and he relishes it. The speech brims with energy and rhetorical command. Despite his villainy—or perhaps because of it—audiences are drawn to Richard. He is among Shakespeare's most compelling villains precisely because he admits to his own monstrosity.
